done.what: A keyframe is the whole terminal as data: both screens, a scrollback tail (or all of it), cursors and saved cursors with pending wrap, modes, palette, cursor style, tab stops, scroll region, charsets, title stack, and the character a repeat sequence would repeat. Cells are written straight into the grid; only state the terminal keeps private goes through its own handlers. Chosen over re-emitting escape sequences because a grid holds things printing cannot make (a soft-wrap flag on any row, an orphaned half of a wide character, a tab cell, a pending wrap on a saved cursor)

A past screen carries 120 rows of scrollback plus whatever the replayed tail scrolled, not the session's whole scrollback. A viewer more than that much taller than the session, or a change of width while a line longer than that tail is in the scrollback, makes the seek start over from the beginning of the journal (correct, slow: served 'full'; 534 ms for all of j100).
Keyframes need a point of rest. Output whose records rarely end at one, or a synchronized update left open, gets fewer keyframes: slower seeks there, never wrong ones.

A replay is what was displayed to within the window's own scheduling: it shows a synchronized update when it closes or 150 ms after it was begun, by the journal's clock (the daemon's, when it recorded the bytes). The window went by its own clock and only stops waiting when no output is queued, so under a flood it may have held an update a little longer than a replay does. Resizes are applied where the journal recorded them, which is when the daemon heard of them.

The past ends at the journal's last flush, not at the live screen: the daemon flushes after 250 ms of quiet or when its 64 KB buffer fills, so while output is arriving 'one step back' starts slightly behind what is on screen.

find does not see text painted and erased inside one record with no line feed between (a full-screen program redrawing in one write). Case folding is done row by row. A hit's `row` and `line` are those of the first line holding the text; while one occurrence or another is on screen it is one stretch.

Stepping into the past reads every record header on the UI thread (76 ms at 122 MB, measured) and holds 20 bytes per record while there (65 MB for 3.26 million records, computed from the table's layout, not measured).
No selection or copy in the past screen: there the mouse only drags the playhead. The 'unavailable' notice covers the last grid row for 2.6 s.
If the session ends while the window is in the past, the window closes as it always has.
Keyframes assume the kitty keyboard protocol stays off (it is off in term::vt_config). Turning it on means carrying the keyboard mode stacks in the snapshot.
Hyperlinks without an id get a per-process number from the terminal; comparisons treat such links as equal when their addresses are, and a restored one keeps its recorded number.
The sidecar is not compressed (5.5% of the journal at 122 MB) and is not counted toward journal_max_mb.
`recall record --cmd` splits on spaces; a command with quoted arguments needs a script file.

The storm is generated input, not a recording. It reached two things no recorded journal here does: the terminal's stale row bookkeeping after widening (now fixed in resize_term) and a restore bug with an alternate screen that had been cleared to a colour (fixed).

On the alternate screen the three rows the bar takes are cut from the past screen, and so are any rows the viewer is short of: from the bottom, where full-screen programs keep their status and input lines, unless the cursor is down there (seen in a picture: vim at 120x36 in a 120x29 view loses its status line; less keeps its prompt and loses its top rows). There is no scrollback behind that screen to bring them back with.

Focus changes are still reported to a program that asked for them while the window is in the past, and a resized window is still reported: the brief says nothing is sent. Both are true events of the live session and were left as the builder wrote them; keys, paste, mouse and wheel are not sent (read in src/app.rs: every path to the program either leaves the past first or returns before it).

A mouse button held when the past is entered by keyboard is released into the past: the program (if it tracks the mouse) never hears the release, and a selection in progress stays 'in progress' until the next click. Not fixed: nothing in the window path can be tested here.
The key that returns from the past is delivered to the program (so is Ctrl+C when nothing is selected). Esc is the way back that sends nothing.

The first seek into a long journal with no index builds it as far as it seeks, and nothing is saved until that seek ends (0.5 s to the middle of 122 MB; all keyframes are held in memory meanwhile, 5.5% of the journal).

Tests whose point depends on a script's pauses (the synchronized-update ones) record again, up to four times, when a busy machine stretches a pause past what they need, and fail with a plain message after that. Tests that need a resize or a keyframe to land in a certain stretch still fail outright if it does not ('nothing to test'); none did in twelve runs here with other lanes compiling.

The first read of a sidecar after it has been written is slow here: opening the file took 65.7 ms against 0.05 ms for the next read (measured with a probe; the slowest seek of each soak run, 66 to 108 ms, is this), most likely the system scanning a file that just changed. One past screen arrives that much later, on the worker thread; `recall bench` does not show it because it builds first and times seeks afterwards.

next.what: Attach from a keyframe instead of the whole journal. What it takes: (1) a full-scrollback snapshot of 'now', which Replay::snapshot(usize::MAX) already gives (3.4 MB, 49 ms to take, 74 ms to restore at 50000x160, against 533 ms to replay 122 MB); (2) someone to hold the terminal it is taken from: the daemon would keep a tracked Replay per session fed from its pump (0.16 microseconds per record here, plus the memory of a grid with scrollback), or rebuild one from the journal's start on first attach and keep it; index keyframes cannot seed it because they hold only a scrollback tail; (3) a new frame type for the snapshot, sent only to windows that ask for it with a byte after the session id in the attach request (older daemons read only the first 8 bytes) so the protocol number stays; (4) Replay::restore taking the window's real listener instead of the silent one, and Terminal adopting the restored terminal together with its primed parser; (5) records after the snapshot's journal offset sent as today
Select and copy in the past screen
find across keyframe segments on several cores, and from the window (jump the playhead to a hit)
Keep the record table out of memory (two levels, or in the sidecar) and scan it off the UI thread
For journal.quota: a third of a flood journal is record headers; merging records in the pump or a varint header would shrink journals and speed every replay
Show a full-screen program's whole past screen while scrubbing: draw the past at the session's own rows (scaled, or the bar over a translucent strip) instead of refitting it to three rows fewer

Run the window path once with a person at the keys, then give it a headless test: the event loop's decisions (what a key does in the past, what reaches the program) pulled out as pure functions the way scrub::wake_draws was

Save keyframes as they are made during a long first build, not at its end; and keep one read handle on the sidecar per index instead of opening it for every keyframe (the open after a write is what costs 66 to 108 ms)
